The Explanation defines foreign company as one incorporated or registered in any form outside Pakistan regardless of whether it has a place of business, business activity or liaison office in Pakistan. s.452(2): the company submits the information to the registrar with its annual return. s.452(3): any investment by a Pakistani company in a foreign company or body corporate is also reported with the annual return. s.452(5): contravention is an offence with a level 1 fine, and the registrar makes an order specifying time to comply. s.452(6): failure to comply with that order is punishable with imprisonment up to three years and a fine up to five hundred thousand rupees, or both. s.452(8): the Commission shall provide the information to the Federal Board of Revenue or any other agency, authority or court.
source: Companies Act 2017 s.452, read verbatim from research/raw/coa2017.txt
note: MAJOR and entirely absent from our guides until now. Three things make it sharp: the thirty-day clock runs from acquiring the interest rather than from any filing season, so it is breached long before an annual return is due; the Explanation is drafted expressly to catch a foreign entity with ZERO Pakistan nexus, overriding the narrower s.2(35) definition; and s.452(8) pipes the register straight to FBR, which connects it to the s.116A obligation. Note the personal duty in s.452(1) is triggered by being a substantial shareholder or officer OF A PAKISTANI COMPANY: a freelancer with a US LLC and no Pakistani company is not caught by that limb. A substantial shareholder is 10 percent or more under the s.2(7) Explanation. VINTAGE CAVEAT: read from a consolidation dated 7 October 2022; secondary reporting describes a 2020 relaxation and reversion, and post-2022 amendments were not checked.

claim: s.102(1): 'Any foreign-source salary received by a resident individual shall be exempt from tax if the individual has paid foreign income tax in respect of the salary.' s.102(2) deems the tax paid where it has been withheld by the employer and paid to the revenue authority of the foreign country in which the employment was exercised. The relief is therefore conditional on foreign tax ACTUALLY having been paid.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.102
note: CRITICAL INTERACTION for Guide A and it is precisely the Gulf case. A Pakistani salaried in the UAE, Saudi Arabia or Qatar pays no foreign income tax, so s.102 gives him NOTHING, and s.103 foreign tax credit likewise gives nothing since there is no foreign tax to credit. The zero-tax country that makes clause 82(d) hard to escape is the same fact that disables the two ordinary reliefs. That leaves s.51(2), which is not conditioned on foreign tax paid and is the provision that actually helps him. This is the analytical spine of Guide A: the reliefs a reader would expect to rescue him are exactly the ones a zero-tax posting switches off.

claim: s.101(1): salary is Pakistan-source income to the extent it '(a) is received from any employment exercised in Pakistan, wherever paid; or (b) is paid by, or on behalf of, the Federal Government, a Provincial Government, or a Local Government in Pakistan, wherever the employment is exercised.' s.101(2): business income of a RESIDENT person is Pakistan-source to the extent derived from a business carried on in Pakistan. s.101(3): business income of a NON-RESIDENT is Pakistan-source to the extent attributable to a permanent establishment in Pakistan, among other limbs.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.101
note: Answers a question both guides need and that readers reliably get wrong: salary is sourced where the EMPLOYMENT IS EXERCISED, 'wherever paid'. So a Pakistani working abroad whose salary is paid into a Pakistani account has FOREIGN-source salary, and a freelancer sitting in Lahore invoicing a US client has PAKISTAN-source business income no matter where the client or the bank is. This is the cleanest way to make the Guide B point that the route the money travels does not determine the tax.

claim: There is no prescribed form for the s.111(4) encashment certificate. A full-text search of the Income Tax Rules 2002 (FBR Income Tax Manual Part II, 248 pages) returns NO rule mentioning encashment, and the only rules made for the purposes of s.111 are rule 228, which prescribes how immovable property, motor cars and jeeps are VALUED for the purposes of s.111. Section 111(5) does empower the Board to make rules under s.237 for the purposes of the section, but no rule prescribing the form or content of the bank certificate appears to have been made. The statute itself asks only for 'a certificate from such bank... to that effect', and FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations calls it a 'certificate of encashment' without prescribing its form.
source: Income Tax Rules 2002 full text search; Income Tax Ordinance s.111(4) and (5); FBR Circular No. 05 of 2022-Operations
note: ANSWERS B2, and the honest answer is that the gap readers complain about is real and statutory, not a failure of their bank. The law names a certificate without defining it, so what a bank issues is a matter of banking practice rather than a prescribed tax form. VINTAGE CAVEAT: the FBR-hosted copy searched carries amendments to about December 2015, so the negative finding is safe for rule 228 and for the absence of any encashment rule as at that date, but a later rule cannot be excluded from this document alone. Before publishing the flat statement 'no prescribed form exists', re-run the search against a current consolidation of the Rules. The positive part of the finding, that rule 228 is about valuation, is unaffected.

claim: s.115(3) verbatim: 'The following persons shall not be required to furnish a return of income for a tax year solely by reason of sub-clause (iii), (iv), (v) and (vi) of clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 114 - (a) A widow; (b) an orphan below the age of twenty-five years; (c) a disabled person; or (d) in the case of ownership of immovable property, a non-resident person.' The relief is therefore confined to the PROPERTY and MOTOR VEHICLE triggers in s.114(1)(b)(iii) to (vi). It does NOT extend to sub-clause (vii), having obtained a National Tax Number. A footnote records that the Finance Act 2008 substituted the present list for the wider original words 'sub-clauses (iii) through (vii)', which had included the NTN trigger.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.115(3) and footnote 3
note: ANSWERS A4 PRECISELY, and the legislative history is the strongest part. Until 2008 a non-resident WAS relieved from filing merely by reason of holding an NTN, and the Finance Act 2008 removed sub-clause (vii) from that relief. So on the face of the Ordinance a non-resident who holds an NTN and owns nothing in Pakistan is still caught by s.114(1)(b)(vii) with no carve-out. Also note s.115(3)(d) is expressly limited to 'the case of ownership of immovable property', which is narrower even than (iii) to (vi) and does not obviously cover the motor vehicle trigger in (vi). This is a genuinely useful, checkable point that competitors miss.

claim: The Federal Tax Ombudsman Secretariat publishes 'Income Tax Laws with Reference to Overseas Pakistanis', prepared by Muhammad Naseer Butt, Advisor Income Tax, as an initiative of the Overseas Pakistanis Grievances Redressal Cell. It states s.82 CORRECTLY, listing the 183-day test, the government-employee-posted-abroad test, and both limbs of clause (d), and makes no mention of the repealed 120-day test.
source: Federal Tax Ombudsman Secretariat, Income Tax Laws with Reference to Overseas Pakistanis
note: Worth contrasting with FBR's own s.82 page, which prints the repealed 120-day clause and omits clause (d) entirely. Two arms of the same state, one right and one five years stale, is a strong and fair illustration for the guide of why vintage checking matters. The FTO document is undated on its face, so cite it for its statements of law rather than for currency, and note it references the pre-Finance-Act-2026 form of clause (114A), listing FCVA and NRVA only.

claim: The FTO overseas guide summarises non-resident filing as follows: a non-resident individual is NOT required to file by reason of owning immovable property of 500 square yards or more, a flat of 2000 square feet or more in a rating area, or a motor vehicle above 1000cc, citing s.115(3)(d); a non-resident individual with the Pakistan-source income listed in clause (114A) of Part IV of the Second Schedule, where the assets were purchased from FCVA or NRVA proceeds, is not required to file; and 'Non-Resident individual earning Pakistan Source Income other than mentioned above is required to file tax return', citing s.114(1)(ab) read with s.101.
source: Federal Tax Ombudsman Secretariat, Income Tax Laws with Reference to Overseas Pakistanis, section A Furnishing of Return
note: The clearest official statement found of the non-resident filing position, and it is directly usable in Guide A. Note the FTO document cites s.115(3)(d) as covering the flat and motor vehicle cases too, whereas the statutory words of s.115(3)(d) are expressly limited to 'the case of ownership of immovable property'. Flag that as a possible over-statement in the FTO summary rather than repeating it, and rely on the statute for the boundary. Note too that this summary, like FBR's FAQ, does not address the NTN trigger in s.114(1)(b)(vii).

claim: s.236K(4): 'Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a scheme introduced by the Federal Government, or Provincial Government or an Authority established under a Federal or Provincial law for expatriate Pakistanis: Provided that the mode of payment by the expatriate Pakistanis in the said scheme or schemes shall be in the foreign exchange remitted from outside Pakistan through normal banking channels.'

Good contrast material for Guide B against s.111(4), where the route buys silence on source rather than a rate.

claim: s.236I(6), added by the Finance Act 2021, exempts a non-resident from advance tax on educational institution fees where he '(i) furnishes copy of passport as an evidence to the educational institution that during previous tax year, his stay in Pakistan was less than one hundred eighty-three days; (ii) furnishes a certificate that he has no Pakistan-source income; and (iii) the fee is remitted directly from abroad through normal banking channels to the bank account of the educational institution.'
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.236I(6)
note: VALUABLE FOR GUIDE A's proof-of-non-residence section, because it is the one place in the Ordinance where Parliament actually SPECIFIED what evidence of non-residence looks like: a copy of the passport plus a self-certificate of no Pakistan-source income. It shows the drafter's expectation that a passport is the ordinary proof, which is the nearest thing to an answer on evidence anywhere in the statute. Two honest caveats for the guide: it is drafted for one narrow withholding provision and does not govern s.82, and it uses the 183-day presence test only, so it does not engage clause (d) at all.

claim: The certificate s.111(4) calls for is issued in practice as the Proceeds Realization Certificate (PRC), and it is prescribed not by FBR but by the State Bank. SBP FE Circular No. 05 of 5 August 2022 wrote it into Foreign Exchange Manual Chapter 10 'Inward and Outward Remittances' at paragraph 2A, with standard formats at Annexure V-148 (e-PRC) and V-149 (Statement of PRCs), updated by EPD Circular Letter No. 02 of 12 June 2025. Chapter 10 para 2A sits under inward remittances immediately before the Home Remittances paragraphs and covers realisation of funds received from abroad generally.
source: SBP Foreign Exchange Manual Chapter 10 para 2A; SBP FE Circular No. 05 of 5 August 2022; bank product pages at HBL, Bank AL Habib, UBL, JS Bank, Bank of Khyber, Allied Bank
note: ANSWERS B2 and closes the practical gap the caller identified. The publishable insight: the Ordinance demands a certificate, FBR holds the rule-making power under s.111(5) and never exercised it, and SBP filled the vacuum. That is why a reader searching FBR for a form number finds nothing. IMPORTANT CORRECTION to our working assumption, which the researching agent initially shared and then refuted: the PRC is NOT export-only. Chapter 12 EXPORTS uses the qualified term 'Export Proceeds Realization Certificate', a species of the genus. Guide B must not tell readers the PRC is an export document. Practical script for the reader: ask for the e-PRC for the specific credit, plus the Statement of PRCs (S-PRC) for the tax year, since s.111(4) tests a per-tax-year aggregate. CAVEAT: Annexure V-148 itself was not read, so do not publish an exact field list for the e-PRC.

claim: The Roshan Digital Account was inaugurated on 10 September 2020 (SBP press release ERD/M&PRD/PR/01/2020-95). There is no single RDA launching circular: RDA is a product wrapper over two account types created a month earlier, the NRVA by SBP FE Circular No. 01 of 2020 and the FCVA by FE Circular No. 02 of 2020, both dated 5 August 2020. Eligibility covers non-resident Pakistanis holding a Pakistani passport, NICOP, POC or NIC, and foreign nationals and foreign companies. A resident Pakistani with FBR-declared foreign assets may open an FCVA but NOT an NRVA.
source: SBP press release 10 September 2020; SBP FE Circulars 01 and 02 of 2020; SBP RDA FAQ
note: Answers B3. Do not invent an RDA circular number, a trap the researching agent flagged explicitly. The resident/non-resident asymmetry on FCVA versus NRVA is the detail most coverage misses and it dovetails with s.152(5AB), which taxes a RESIDENT citizen with declared foreign assets investing through an FCVA at 10 percent final.

claim: SBP EPD Circular Letter No. 05 of 24 March 2026 broadens the value accounts so that all non-resident persons, natural or juridical, as defined under the Income Tax Ordinance 2001, are eligible, and confirms the two business variants FCBVA and NRBVA for juridical persons, excluding sole proprietorships and unregistered partnerships. Under the current rules FCVA is open to all non-resident individuals plus resident individual Pakistanis holding declared foreign assets per the latest FBR wealth statement; NRVA is for non-resident individuals only. Both accounts permit remittances and payments outside Pakistan to the extent of the balance without any prior approval from the bank or the State Bank, with one carve-out: on real estate disinvestment the principal is repatriable at any time but capital gain only after three years.
source: SBP EPD Circular Letter No. 05 of 2026, 24 March 2026, Annexures A and B
note: Answers B4 from SBP's side and CONFIRMS the caller's already-verified s.236C FCVA/NRVA point from the regulator's direction. Note how neatly the SBP and FBR timelines interlock: SBP widened the accounts to juridical persons in March 2026 and the Finance Act 2026 three months later added FCBVA and NRBVA to clause (79), clause (111AB), clause (114A) and s.152(1DA). That is a strong, fully sourced narrative for Guide B. The three-year capital gain repatriation lock is a genuinely practical point that most coverage omits.

claim: Inward remittances are not a reporting category in the bank-reporting provisions. s.165A requires banks to report cash withdrawals over Rs 50,000 per day aggregating Rs 1 million or more monthly, deposits aggregating Rs 10 million or more monthly, credit card payments of Rs 200,000 or more monthly, recipients of profit on debt annually, and business accounts opened or re-designated. A search of ss.165, 165A, 165AB, 165B and 165C for 'remitt' returns no hits. A remittance is caught only incidentally, if it pushes an account over the deposit threshold. There is no standalone filing obligation on the individual recipient of a remittance.
source: Income Tax Ordinance ss.165 to 165C
note: Answers the reporting half of B and corrects a widespread anxiety in the diaspora that every remittance is reported to FBR by name. The honest framing is that the recipient has no reporting duty, the duty is evidentiary, but the money is far from invisible: s.165AB inserted by the Finance Act 2026 puts bank and EMI data into a Central Data Hub for algorithmic cross-matching where deposits or withdrawals exceed Rs 100 million in a six-month period, s.175AA provides FBR-bank cross-matching, and s.165B carries CRS automatic exchange of information reporting on non-resident and reportable persons.

claim: s.165AB, inserted by the Finance Act 2026, verified verbatim in the consolidated Ordinance. Notwithstanding the Banking Companies Ordinance 1962, the State Bank of Pakistan Act 1956, the Protection of Economic Reforms Act 1992 or any other law, every banking company and Electronic Money Institution shall electronically upload information to the Central Data Hub for algorithmic cross-matching of tax and bank information. Sub-section (2) covers account holders having deposits OR withdrawals exceeding one hundred million Rupees during a reporting period in any or all accounts, specifying deposits or withdrawals including opening and closing balances, peak credits and total credits. Sub-section (3): the information shall be digitally processed and shall NOT be visible to any Income Tax Authority during cross-matching. Sub-section (4): on gross mismatch the information feeds the Compliance Risk Management system and proceedings are conducted by the National faceless centre. A reporting period is a six-month period, July to December or January to June, with specified dates of 31 January and 31 July.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.165AB and footnote 8
note: Independently verified against the primary source rather than taken second hand. Note the override expressly names the Protection of Economic Reforms Act 1992, the statute behind the foreign currency account protections, which is significant given Zaidi's argument about that regime. The Rs 100 million threshold is far above ordinary diaspora remittance levels, so the honest line for Guide B is that this is not aimed at the family remittance, while noting the direction of travel. The confidentiality and not-visible-to-officers safeguards should be reported alongside the surveillance, not omitted.

claim: CORRECTION to a subagent report which stated two years. FERA 1947 s.23(1): a person who contravenes, attempts to contravene or abets the contravention of the Act (other than the listed excepted provisions) shall, notwithstanding the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, be tried by a Tribunal constituted under s.23A and shall be punishable with RIGOROUS IMPRISONMENT for a term which may extend to FIVE YEARS or with fine or with both, and the Tribunal may in addition direct confiscation of the currency, security, gold or silver, goods or other property in respect of which the contravention took place. By s.23(2) the offence is cognizable and non-bailable. By s.23(3) a Tribunal shall not take cognizance except upon a written complaint by a person authorised by the State Bank. s.4(1) restricts dealing in foreign exchange by anyone other than an authorised dealer without SBP permission, and s.5(1) restricts payments to or for the credit of persons resident outside Pakistan.
source: Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947, ss.4, 5 and 23, read from the local copy at research/raw/fera-1947.txt
note: CORRECTS a second-hand figure before it reached a guide. The subagent reported 'up to two years imprisonment, or fine, or both'; the statute says rigorous imprisonment up to five years. Read verbatim from the primary text. Two further details worth publishing because they change the practical picture: the offence is cognizable and NON-BAILABLE, and prosecution requires a written complaint by a person authorised by the State Bank, so it is not something a tax officer initiates. Guide B can use this to make the point that using an unofficial channel risks an exchange-control offence that is entirely separate from, and cumulative with, losing the s.111(4) protection.

claim: SUPERSEDES the earlier finding s82-no-day-counting-rule, which was WRONG. The day-counting rule exists, in the Income Tax RULES 2002 rather than the Ordinance. Rule 14 'Resident individual' applies for the purposes of s.82 and provides, in computing the number of days an individual is present in Pakistan in a tax year: (a) subject to clause (c), a part of a day that an individual is present in Pakistan, INCLUDING THE DAY OF ARRIVAL IN AND THE DAY OF DEPARTURE FROM PAKISTAN, counts as a whole day of such presence; (b) the following days in which an individual is wholly or partly present in Pakistan count as a whole day: a public holiday, a day of leave including sick leave, a day the individual's activity in Pakistan is interrupted because of a strike, lock-out or delay in receipt of supplies, or a holiday spent in Pakistan before, during or after any activity in Pakistan; and (c) A DAY OR PART OF A DAY WHERE AN INDIVIDUAL IS IN PAKISTAN SOLELY BY REASON OF BEING IN TRANSIT between two different places outside Pakistan DOES NOT COUNT as a day present in Pakistan. A footnote records that the words 'of clauses (a) and (b)' were omitted from sub-rule (2) by SRO 392(I)/2009 dated 19 May 2009.
source: Income Tax Rules 2002, rule 14, verified in two separate FBR consolidations
note: CORRECTS OUR OWN ERROR before publication, and the error is instructive enough to be worth a line in the guide's method: we searched the ORDINANCE, found nothing, and nearly published 'the statute is silent' as an open question. The rule was in the RULES all along. It also UPGRADES the Zaidi statement recorded as arrival-departure-days-count-secondary from tier 3 practice to tier 1 law: rule 14(2)(a) says exactly that, so it can now be published as law. Verified in two independently fetched consolidations, so the finding does not rest on one document's vintage. The transit carve-out in (c) is genuinely useful and almost never mentioned in diaspora coverage.

claim: Rule 14 computes only the number of days an individual is present IN PAKISTAN, for the purposes of s.82. It provides no method for counting days spent in a third country. Clause 82(d) turns on whether a citizen of Pakistan was 'present in any other country for more than one hundred and eighty-two days during the tax year', a computation for which neither the Ordinance nor the Rules supplies any rule, evidential standard or procedure.
source: Income Tax Rules 2002 rule 14, read against s.82(d)
note: THE OPEN QUESTION SURVIVES, but in a much sharper and better-evidenced form than before. It is not that Pakistan has no day-counting rule; it is that Pakistan has a detailed day-counting rule for presence in Pakistan and NONE for the third-country test that clause (d) depends on. That asymmetry is checkable by any reader and supports Zaidi's separate point that clause (d) is 'not implementable as staying in another country for certain days falls outside Pakistan's regulatory system'.

claim: Pakistan-UAE tax treaty, signed 7 February 1993, in force 30 November 1994, effective in Pakistan from 1 July 1995. Article 4(1) verbatim: 'For the purposes of this Convention, the term "resident of a Contracting State" means any person who, under the laws of that State, operates an industrial or commercial establishment, or is liable to tax therein by reason of his domicile, residence, place of management or any other criterion of a similar nature.' Article 4(2) then supplies a standard four-step tie-breaker for dual-resident individuals: permanent home; centre of vital interests; habitual abode; nationality; then mutual agreement. FBR's MLI-synthesized text leaves Article 4 unchanged.
source: FBR published Pakistan-UAE Income Tax Convention; FBR MLI-synthesized text
note: Read verbatim from FBR's own PDF, and the caller's suspicion about a special UAE definition is CORRECT but not in the form usually claimed. The 'operates an industrial or commercial establishment' limb is an ESTABLISHMENT-based alternative to liability to tax. It is NOT a nationality or residence deeming provision of the kind found in some other UAE treaties. So a salaried Pakistani employee in the UAE neither operates an establishment nor is straightforwardly 'liable to tax' in a state with no personal income tax, and the Article 4(2) tie-breaker may never engage for him at all, because it only operates where a person is a resident of both states under Article 4(1). Two independent research streams converged on this separately. No tier 1 or tier 2 source resolves it. THIS IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE OPEN QUESTION IN GUIDE A.

claim: The Pakistan-United States income tax treaty in force is the 1957 Convention, in force 21 May 1959. It contains NO residency tie-breaker article: the terms 'permanent home', 'centre of vital interests' and 'habitual abode' do not appear anywhere in the text. Its definitions are mutually exclusive by construction, defining a resident of Pakistan as a person 'who is resident in Pakistan for the purposes of Pakistan tax and not resident in the United States for the purposes of the United States tax'.
source: FBR published Pakistan-United States Income Tax Convention 1957
note: Independently verified by grepping FBR's own PDF: zero occurrences of any tie-breaker phrase. The consequence is sharp and publishable: because the definitions exclude each other rather than resolve a conflict, a dual resident falls OUTSIDE both definitions instead of being allocated to one state. A Pakistani-American caught by s.82(d) therefore has no treaty tie-breaker to invoke. This is the opposite of the reassurance most diaspora coverage offers about treaties, and it is checkable in seconds.

claim: Treaty position for the main diaspora destinations, from FBR's own treaty pages: UNITED KINGDOM, 1986 convention in force 8 December 1987, MLI-modified, standard four-step Article 4 tie-breaker. UNITED STATES, 1957 convention in force 21 May 1959, NO tie-breaker. UAE, 1993 convention in force 30 November 1994, MLI-modified, tie-breaker present but resting on the non-standard Article 4(1) definition. SAUDI ARABIA, 2006 convention, SRO 1194(I)/2006, standard tie-breaker. CANADA, 1976 convention in force 15 December 1977, tie-breaker in Article IV headed Fiscal Domicile. AUSTRALIA, NO comprehensive tax treaty with Pakistan: Australia appears in none of FBR's three treaty categories, full-scope, limited-purpose or MLI-synthesized.
source: FBR Double Taxation Agreements pages and published treaty PDFs
note: Answers A6's list requirement. The two surprises are the ones worth leading with: the US treaty is from 1957 and has no tie-breaker, and Australia has no treaty at all, so a Pakistani in Australia caught by clause (d) has no treaty relief route whatsoever and must rely on domestic provisions such as s.51(2) or s.102. Note the structural point that a tie-breaker only engages where the person is a resident of BOTH states under their domestic laws, which is exactly what a zero-tax state can defeat.

claim: Rule 19A of the Income Tax Rules 2002, 'Certificate of residence', runs in ONE DIRECTION ONLY: it is machinery for a person RESIDENT IN PAKISTAN to obtain a Pakistani certificate of residence for presentation abroad. There is no counterpart rule prescribing what a taxpayer must produce to prove FOREIGN residency to FBR, and the phrase 'resident taxpayer of any other country' appears nowhere in the Rules.
source: Income Tax Rules 2002, rule 19A and full-text search
note: ANSWERS A3 and it is a clean, checkable negative. A tax residency certificate is not legally REQUIRED to establish the second limb of clause 82(d), because nothing is prescribed at all; and by the same token nothing is guaranteed to be ACCEPTED. Combined with the FBR Overseas FAQ, which asks only for documents 'in support thereof' subject to a Commissioner's approval, the honest published answer is that the evidential standard is undefined and discretionary. Vintage caveat: FBR's newest published consolidated Rules is amended to 24.11.2023.

claim: The premise that a Pakistani in a zero-income-tax Gulf state cannot obtain a tax residency certificate is FALSE. All three main destinations issue them to individuals. UAE: under Cabinet Decision No. 85 of 2022 article 4, a natural person qualifies via a 183-day limb, or a 90-day limb combined with UAE nationality or a residence permit plus a permanent place of residence or employment, or a primary-residence-and-centre-of-financial-and-personal-interests limb; the 183-day route requires only an Emirates ID or passport plus an ICP entry-exit report. SAUDI ARABIA: ZATCA operates a dedicated certificate service for individuals, free, requiring passport, proof of residency and an employment verification letter, with the Income Tax Law article 3 test being a permanent abode plus 30 days, or 183 days. QATAR: the Dhareeba manual states expressly that non-registered natural persons may apply, with an employer letter mandatory.
source: UAE Cabinet Decision No. 85 of 2022 and UAE FTA service card; ZATCA eServices individuals certificate service; Qatar Dhareeba user manual
note: CORRECTS THE CALLER'S OWN WORKING PREMISE, which is the most useful kind of finding. The reason these certificates are obtainable is structural and worth explaining: UAE, Saudi and Qatari residency tests turn on PRESENCE AND ABODE, not on liability to tax, so the absence of a personal income tax is not a bar to certification. The real gap is on Pakistan's side, where nothing obliges FBR to accept the certificate. Two practical cautions: there is no general 183-day minimum for a UAE TREATY certificate, the requirement depends on the treaty, and the widely repeated contrary claim is vendor-sourced and unverified; and the UAE treaty certificate names the counterparty country, so the applicant must select Pakistan, while the domestic-purposes certificate names none, and choosing the wrong type wastes a non-refundable fee.

claim: FBR's operational guidance for overseas Pakistanis consistently uses the 183-day presence test alone and never mentions clause 82(d). FBR Circular No. 3 of 2023-24 dated 15 August 2023, operationalising s.7E for overseas Pakistanis, instructs transferring authorities to verify that 'the non-resident person stay in Pakistan is less than 183 days'. FBR's Overseas Pakistanis FAQ frames non-residence the same way. The Finance Act 2023 explanatory circular (Circular 2 of 2023) and Circular 01 of 2025-26 contain zero mentions of s.82 or residency.
source: FBR Circular No. 3 of 2023-24; FBR Overseas Pakistanis FAQ; FBR explanatory circulars for the Finance Acts 2023 and 2025
note: Reinforces the A5 answer from a second direction. Beyond the single paraphrasing paragraph in Circular 15 of 2022-23, FBR has said nothing about clause (d) in four years, and its own operational instructions proceed as though only the 183-day test exists. Consultant confidence about clause (d) is therefore not traceable to FBR. One honest gap to preserve: Circular 01 of 2024-25 is a scanned image PDF with no text layer and was NOT searched, so it is recorded as unchecked rather than as a negative.

claim: There is no route onto the Active Taxpayers List without filing a return. Rule 81B of the Income Tax Rules keys ATL inclusion solely to the filing of a return, and s.181A delegates the mechanics to rules. What DOES exist is filer TREATMENT without ATL membership, in two forms: Second Schedule Part IV clause (111AC), which disapplies s.100BA and rule 1 of the Tenth Schedule for a non-resident individual holding a POC or NICOP in respect of s.236C and s.236K transactions and is not conditioned on holding any bank account; and the operational PSID route in FBR's Overseas Pakistanis FAQ, where a Commissioner approves filer-rate payment after verifying uploaded documents.
source: Income Tax Rules rule 81B; Income Tax Ordinance s.181A; Second Schedule Part IV clause (111AC); FBR Overseas Pakistanis FAQ
note: Answers A4(iv) and draws a distinction most coverage blurs: being ON the ATL and being TAXED AT FILER RATES are different things, and an overseas Pakistani can get the second without the first. Also corrects a plausible misconception: the Tenth Schedule itself contains no non-resident exclusion, the word does not appear in it; the relief sits in the Second Schedule. OPEN ITEM: SRO 1638(I)/2024, the final version of the rule 81B amendment, could not be retrieved and only the draft SRO 1448(I)/2024 is in hand, so do not quote rule 81B verbatim.

claim: SUPERSEDED AND WITHDRAWN. Our record s111-4-cap-was-added stated that the Rs 5 million cap in s.111(4) 'arrived later and appears in the sub-section as substituted by the Finance Act 2021', implying the cap itself was a 2021 creation and that the shield was unlimited from 2004 to 2021. That reading was wrong.
source: Self-correction against s111-4-cap-history-resolved and FBR Circular No. 05
note: THE READING ERROR IS THE LESSON. The Ordinance footnote says the Finance Act 2021 SUBSTITUTED sub-section (4), and the substituted text reproduced in the footnote ALREADY CONTAINED the five million figure with its own nested footnotes. Text quoted inside a footnote is the OLD version, not the new one, and we read the nested history as though the outermost amendment introduced everything in it. The correct history is: no limit until 2018, Rs 10 million by the Finance Act 2018, Rs 5 million by the Finance Act 2019, restructured without change by the Finance Act 2021. The published guide has been corrected. Generalise the rule: when a footnote reproduces substituted text, read the nested footnotes before attributing any wording in it to the substituting Act.

claim: s.15A(1)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 allows, in computing income chargeable under the head Income from Property, a deduction for 'any local rate, tax, charge or cess in respect of the property or the rent from the property paid or payable by the person to any local authority or government in the year, NOT BEING any tax payable under this Ordinance'. Provincial urban immovable property tax is a tax in respect of the property payable to a government and is not a tax payable under the Ordinance, so it falls squarely inside the deduction and outside the carve-out.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.15A(1)(c), read verbatim and cross-checked against the second consolidation on disk
note: THE CROSS-REGIME POINT nobody writes. Provincial property tax and federal income tax are separate charges levied by separate authorities, and the only place they touch is here: the provincial tax reduces the federal rental income base. Note the express carve-out 'not being any tax payable under this Ordinance', which is what stops someone deducting their own income tax. Other deductions in the same sub-section worth stating alongside it: (a) a flat one-fifth repair allowance on the rent, (e) profit on money borrowed to acquire, construct, renovate, extend or reconstruct, and (h) up to four per cent of rent for administration and collection, reduced from six per cent by the Finance Act 2020.

claim: s.15A applies to a 'person', not only to a company, and this is settled from the footnotes themselves rather than inferred from marker order. Footnote 5 reads 'The word "person" substituted by the Finance Act, 2016' and footnote 6 reads 'The word "company" substituted by the Finance Act, 2021'. In this consolidation's convention the quoted word is the word REPLACED, so the Finance Act 2016 replaced 'person' with 'company' and the Finance Act 2021 replaced 'company' back with 'person'. The operative word in the current text is therefore 'person', consistent with s.15(1) charging rent received by 'a person' generally. Independently corroborated: the Finance Act 2022 was downloaded in full and makes no amendment to s.15A, so nothing later disturbs the 2021 position.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, ss.15 and 15A; identical reading confirmed in the second consolidation at research/raw/it-ordinance.txt
note: READ THE FOOTNOTE, NOT THE MARKER ORDER. The first pass inferred from the sequence 5[ ] 6[person] that the Finance Act 2021 had substituted 'company' INTO the text, which would have restricted every s.15A deduction to companies and made the provincial-property-tax deduction useless to an individual landlord: the opposite of the truth. The convention is that a footnote names the word REPLACED. This is a close cousin of the nested-footnote trap in s111-4-cap-was-added-CORRECTED and belongs beside it in METHOD.md. Verified across three consolidations carrying identical text, plus the full Finance Act 2022 confirming no later amendment.

claim: s.155(3) defines prescribed person for rent withholding as: the Federal Government; a Provincial Government; a Local Government; a company; a non-profit organization or charitable institution; a diplomatic mission of a foreign state; a private educational institution, a boutique, a beauty parlour, a hospital, a clinic or a maternity home; individuals or associations of persons paying gross rent of one and a half million rupees and above in a year; and any other person notified by the Board.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.155(3)
note: The category nobody expects is sub-clause (via), inserted by the Finance Act 2013: a boutique, a beauty parlour, a hospital, a clinic or a maternity home is a prescribed person by virtue of WHAT IT IS, with no turnover or rent threshold attached, while an ordinary individual or AOP only becomes one at Rs 1.5 million of gross rent a year. So a small beauty parlour renting a shop must withhold from the first rupee while a far larger individual landlord's tenant need not. Confirms the individualTenantThreshold of 1,500,000 in lib/tax/property.ts.

claim: An Explanation added to s.155(1) by the Finance Act 2021 provides, for removal of doubt, that sub-section (1) applies when a payment is made on account of rent of immovable property IRRESPECTIVE OF HEAD OF INCOME. A separate Explanation inserted by the Finance Act 2006 provides that 'gross amount of rent' includes amounts referred to in s.16(1) or s.16(3), the non-adjustable amounts received in relation to buildings.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.155(1) and its two Explanations
note: The 2021 Explanation closes an argument that used to be run: that rent taxable as business income rather than under the head Income from Property escaped s.155. It does not. The 2006 Explanation matters for anyone taking a large deposit, because s.16 spreads a non-adjustable amount over ten years and that spread amount is inside the gross rent for withholding.

claim: Rent withholding under s.155 is not a final tax. The former s.155(2), which provided that 'the tax deducted under sub-section (1) shall be a final tax on the income from property', was OMITTED by the Finance Act 2010. The deduction is therefore adjustable against the landlord's actual liability computed on the rent slabs, and the landlord still files.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.155 footnote 5 recording the omission of sub-section (2)
note: Sixteen years stale and still repeated. Pages describing rent withholding as a final discharge are quoting a sub-section removed in 2010, which is the same shape as the s.111(4) unlimited-shield error: the source is not inventing it, the source is quoting repealed law. Practical consequence for the guide: a landlord whose tenant withheld cannot treat the matter as closed, and where the slab computation is lower than what was withheld the excess is recoverable only through the return.

claim: s.16(1): where the owner of a building receives from a tenant an amount which is NOT ADJUSTABLE against the rent payable, that amount is treated as rent chargeable under the head Income from Property in the year received AND THE FOLLOWING NINE TAX YEARS IN EQUAL PROPORTION. s.16(2): if the owner refunds it on termination before ten years have expired, no portion is allocated to the year of refund or any later year, except as provided in s.16(3). s.16(3): where the owner then lets to a succeeding tenant and takes a new non-adjustable amount, that succeeding amount REDUCED BY the portion of the earlier amount already charged to tax is treated as rent under s.16(1).
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.16
note: A real and expensive trap for landlords, and it interacts with s.155: the Explanation to s.155(1) inserted by the Finance Act 2006 puts s.16(1) and s.16(3) amounts inside the 'gross amount of rent' from which a prescribed person withholds. So a large non-adjustable deposit is taxable income spread over a decade AND part of the withholding base, not a neutral security held on trust. The s.16(3) mechanism is the part nobody explains: it prevents the same money being taxed twice across successive tenants by netting off what was already charged.

claim: A proviso to s.231B(2) provides that no advance tax shall be collected under that sub-section on the transfer of a vehicle after FIVE YEARS from the date of first registration in Pakistan. s.231B(2) is the transfer-of-registration charge, distinct from s.231B(1) which is collected by the Excise and Taxation registering authority at first registration of a new locally manufactured vehicle.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.231B(2) proviso
note: A clean, checkable and widely omitted point. Buying a car more than five years old attracts no s.231B transfer collection at all, whatever the buyer's filer status, so the filer/non-filer gap that dominates coverage of vehicle tax simply does not arise on an older car. Reconciles with lib/tax/vehicle.ts usedReductionPerYear, which tapers the transfer amount by year of age.

claim: s.231B(2A), inserted after the Finance Act 2016, requires the Excise and Taxation registration authority to collect tax at the Division VII rates at registration where a locally manufactured vehicle HAS BEEN SOLD PRIOR TO REGISTRATION by the person who originally purchased it from the local manufacturer. Separately s.231B(4) provides that sub-section (1) does not apply where the person produces evidence that tax was already collected from the same person under sub-section (3) on a locally manufactured vehicle, or under s.148 on an imported vehicle.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.231B(2A) and (4)
note: Two mechanisms most coverage misses. (2A) is an anti-flipping rule aimed at own-money booking, where a buyer books a car from the manufacturer and sells the allocation before registering it. (4) is the protection against paying twice on the same vehicle: the manufacturer collects under (3) or customs collects under s.148 on import, and producing that evidence disapplies the registration charge under (1). A reader who paid at the showroom and is asked again at registration needs (4).

claim: The proviso to s.231B(1) disapplies the section for the Federal Government, a Provincial Government, a Local Government, a foreign diplomat, and a diplomatic mission in Pakistan. The word 'private' was omitted from the section heading and from sub-section (1) by the Finance Act 2022, so the charge is no longer confined to private motor vehicles.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.231B(1) proviso and footnotes
note: The Finance Act 2022 omission of 'private' is worth stating because the section is still widely titled 'advance tax on private motor vehicles' in secondary coverage, including in the Ordinance's own contents page at line 666, which retains the old heading while the operative text no longer carries the word.

claim: The general pension exemption was REPEALED by the Finance Act 2025. Clause (8) of Part I of the Second Schedule, which exempted 'any pension received by a citizen of Pakistan from a former employer, other than where the person continues to work for the employer', was omitted. Sub-clause (i) of clause (9), which exempted pension for service rendered by a member of the Armed Forces or as an employee of the Federal or a Provincial Government, was also omitted by the Finance Act 2025. What survives in clause (9) is only sub-clause (ii): pension granted under the relevant rules to the FAMILIES AND DEPENDENTS of public servants or members of the Armed Forces who die during service.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, Second Schedule Part I clauses (8) and (9) and their footnotes
note: MAJOR and current. Pension in Pakistan was broadly exempt and is no longer. Almost all published content, and most readers, still work on the old position. Note the survivors: commutation of pension from Government or an approved scheme remains exempt under clause (12), gratuity and commutation on retirement remain exempt within limits under clause (13), and the family pension limb of clause (9)(ii) is untouched. The Finance Act 2026 does not mention pension, so the 2025 position stands for tax year 2027.

claim: s.12(2A), inserted by the Finance Act 2025, is the replacement regime. Pension from a former employer is charged as a FINAL TAX at the rates in the proviso to clause (2) of Division I of Part I of the First Schedule, which reads: 0% where the amount of pension received does not exceed rupees ten million, and 5% of the amount exceeding rupees ten million where it does. s.12(2A)(i) further provides that an individual who has attained the age of SEVENTY YEARS shall not be charged to tax on pension income at all. s.12(2A)(ii): the pension of an individual who continues to work for the former employer or its associate is charged at the ordinary Division I rates instead, under clause (1) or (2) as the case may be.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.12(2A) and First Schedule Part I Division I clause (2) proviso, read from PDF page 528
note: The practical shape, and it is far gentler than 'pension is now taxable' suggests: an ordinary pensioner below Rs 10 million a year pays nothing, and anyone 70 or over pays nothing at any amount. The 5 percent bites only on the excess above Rs 10 million. The genuine sting is s.12(2A)(ii): keep working for the same employer or an associate and the whole pension moves onto the ordinary salary slabs rather than the 0/5 percent table. Interpolate the figures from lib/tax/ if a guide states them; do not retype.

claim: Punjab UIPT is charged under s.3(2) of the Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act 1958 on the TAXABLE VALUE of a building and land at the rate given in the Schedule, not on annual rental value. The Schedule rates are: up to Rs 5m residential Exempt / commercial 0.07%; over Rs 5m to Rs 10m 0.07% both; over Rs 10m to Rs 25m 0.08% both; Rs 25m and above 0.09% both. Taxable value is determined under s.5(1) by the valuation table, and s.2(j) defines valuation table as the table notified under the Stamp Act 1899 (the DC rate).
source: Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act 1958 (V of 1958), ss.2(g-a), 2(j), 3(2), 5, Schedule, current consolidation citing the Punjab Finance Act 2026 (L of 2026); corroborated in the Punjab Finance Act 2024 (VIII of 2024) s.4 gazette text
note: TRAP RECORDED: punjablaws.gov.pk/lawspdf/79.pdf serves a STALE consolidation of the same Act, latest footnote 2013, still printing 'tax on the annual value ... at the rate of ten per cent'. It is a genuinely official source and the wrong vintage. Use excise.punjab.gov.pk/system/files/18.pdf, whose footnotes cite the Punjab Finance Act 2026. The department's OWN page excise.punjab.gov.pk/property_tax is also stale: it still says 5% of annual value and the 5 marla exemption.

claim: The capital-value regime was enacted by s.4 of the Punjab Finance Act 2024 (VIII of 2024), assented 27 June 2024, which by s.1(3) did NOT come into force with the rest of the Act on 1 July 2024 but 'on such date as the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify'. The Schedule's own transitional table pivots on tax payable 'on and before 31.12.2024', which places commencement at 1 January 2025.
source: Punjab Finance Act 2024 (VIII of 2024), ss.1(3) and 4, and the Schedule inserted by s.4(12)
note: The 1 January 2025 date is inferred from the statutory 31.12.2024 pivot plus consistent tier-3 press (Dawn 1930358, Business Recorder, Profit). The commencement NOTIFICATION itself was not located. Publish the date, flag the notification as unlocated.

claim: The Punjab UIPT Schedule contains a second, transitional table almost universally omitted by secondary guides: where the tax under the main table is LOWER than the tax payable on and before 31.12.2024, the taxpayer instead pays the old tax (up to Rs 5m residential: exempt; all other bands: old tax +10%, and +20% for the Rs 25m-and-above band) until the main-table figure catches up. So the capital-value rates are a floor, not a universal reduction, for a property already on the roll before 2025.
source: Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act 1958, Schedule, second table; identical text in Punjab Finance Act 2024 s.4(12)

claim: Punjab UIPT: due yearly on or before 30 September under s.12(1), which since the Punjab Finance Act 2026 requires payment ELECTRONICALLY. A 5% rebate of annual tax is given under s.3(5) if the tax is paid in lump sum on or before 30 September. Late payment surcharge under s.12(3) is 1% of gross payable tax imposed on the first day of October, January, April and July, i.e. QUARTERLY.
source: Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act 1958, ss.3(5), 12(1), 12(3)
note: CORRECTION TARGET: the surcharge was 'every month of delay' until the Punjab Finance Act 2026 (L of 2026) substituted the quarterly wording effective 1 July 2026 (footnote 5 to s.12). Punjab's own excise.punjab.gov.pk/property_tax page and most secondary guides still say 1% MONTHLY. Both the electronic-payment requirement and the quarterly surcharge are 2026 changes.

claim: Punjab s.4(c)(i) now exempts buildings and lands used or intended to be used exclusively as residential whose TAXABLE VALUE does not exceed Rs 5 million. The Punjab Finance Act 2024 s.4(3) OMITTED both the old owner-occupied annual-value exemption in s.4(c)(ii) and the five-marla exemption in s.4(i). The widow, divorcee, disabled person and minor orphan exemption in s.4(g) survives but is still expressed in ANNUAL VALUE not exceeding Rs 243,000, an unconverted relic of the repealed ARV basis.
source: Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act 1958 s.4(c),(g); Punjab Finance Act 2024 s.4(3)
note: OPEN QUESTION worth publishing: the Act gives no conversion rule for reading the s.4(g) annual-value threshold under a regime that no longer computes annual value. Nothing found addressing it.

claim: For Punjab the lookup key is the PIN (Property Identification Number), not the PT-10 number. On ePay Punjab you search by PIN or by PSID; the system returns one or more PT-10 numbers (separate PT-10s for arrears and current year), you select one, verify the property details, then click Generate Challan to produce a 17-18 digit PSID, which is paid at ATMs, internet and mobile banking, mobile wallets or over the counter at any bank in Punjab. The PIN format is 5 digits, a long block, then 2 digits, e.g. 06180-1850200103301203401012345-01.
source: ePay Punjab official Property Tax user guide (storage.epay.punjab.gov.pk); Punjab ETNCD PT-5 online verification system
note: The PT-10 is the CHALLAN the system generates, so 'search by your PT-10 number' is backwards. The user guide is an image-only PDF (no text layer), read by rendering pages with pdftoppm. The department menu item labelled 'System for Online Verification of PT10 Challan' actually opens a PT-5 verification page at http://116.0.52.52:86/ which asks for CNIC plus PIN, and it is plain HTTP on a bare IP. The department's own UIPT Property Tax Calculator at excise.punjab.gov.pk/property-tax-calculator returned 'The Page Under Maintenance will be Available Soon' on 10 Sep 2026.

claim: Provincial Urban Immovable Property Tax paid is an ALLOWABLE DEDUCTION against income from property under s.15A(1)(c) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001, which allows 'any local rate, tax, charge or cess in respect of the property or the rent from the property paid or payable by the person to any local authority or government in the year, not being any tax payable under this Ordinance'. The carve-out excludes only federal income tax under the Ordinance, so provincial property tax is within the deduction. Since the Finance Act 2021 omitted s.15(6), s.15(7) and s.15A(7), s.15A applies to every person with no opt-in and no threshold.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.15A(1)(c), amended up to 30 June 2026
note: Deduction is on a paid-or-payable basis subject to the s.15A(3) three-year clawback for unpaid liabilities, s.15A(5) no double deduction, and s.15A(6) applying s.21. s.155 rent withholding is adjustable not final (the final-tax s.155(2) was omitted by the Finance Act 2010). This is the cross-regime point no published Pakistani guide was found to make.

claim: After the Finance Act 2026 omitted s.7E and its rate Division VIIIC, s.236C(2A) of the Income Tax Ordinance still requires registering or attesting authorities not to record a transfer unless the seller has discharged 'its tax liability under section 7E'. The cross-reference was not repealed with the section, so it now points at an omitted provision.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.236C(2A) as it stands amended up to 30 June 2026; Finance Act 2026 s.5(4) omitting s.7E
note: No liability can arise under an omitted s.7E prospectively, but liability for tax years 2023-2026 was validly incurred while s.7E was live and is not erased. Registration staff may keep asking for a 7E certificate until FBR clarifies. No FBR circular addressing the dangling reference was located.

claim: Punjab has NOT introduced a provincial deemed-income charge to replace the repealed federal s.7E. The only related concept in the Punjab UIPT Act is s.5(3), a power for Government to 'specify and categorize a property as the high value property', with s.2(d-a) defining high value property by reference to it. No separate charge attaches to that categorisation in the Act or Schedule.
source: Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act 1958 ss.2(d-a), 5(3), Schedule
note: Established by reading the whole Act and Schedule rather than by absence of search results. Punjab's separate Luxury House Tax (Punjab Finance Act 2014) is a distinct ONE-TIME charge on houses of 2 kanals+ with 6000+ sq ft covered area, charged in addition to property tax, not a deemed-income tax.

claim: The s.12(2A) pension INCOME regime is not modelled anywhere in lib/tax/. What exists is RELIEF.pensionIncomeRate in lib/tax/pakistan.ts, which is the twenty per cent cap on the s.63 approved-pension-fund CONTRIBUTION credit, an entirely different provision. There is no module holding the 0 percent / 5 percent pension table, the Rs 10 million threshold or the age-seventy exemption, and no check-tax assertion covering them.
source: grep of lib/tax/ against s.12(2A) and the Division I proviso, 10 September 2026
note: BLOCKS a pensioner guide under the project's own no-figures rule: a rate stated in guide prose that no check can see is a second source of truth, and the next Finance Act moves the law without moving the page. Two honest options. Either extend lib/tax/ with the s.12(2A) table plus check-tax assertions and then interpolate, which is the pattern the salary guide already uses, or write the guide without printing the figures and point at the sections. The first is better and is a small change: one table, one threshold, one age rule. Recorded so the next session does not print the numbers into prose by default.
